title: Fractional chief AI officer: what should you walk away with?
description: What a part-time chief AI officer should leave you with. Plus what a full-time seat costs, and when part-time fits a firm of 40 to 500.
verdict: Buy ownership, not advice: a named executive with a budget, authority to stop projects and a review date.[^8][^5]
Part-time ownership is normal: most federal chief AI officers also hold another executive job.[^1][^2]
Firms rarely advertise this seat: in US job ads, fractional finance seats far outnumber AI ones.[^27][^14]
A full-time seat at median US IT-manager pay plus benefits runs about $251,000 to $259,000 a year.[^9][^10]
People keep the calls: the CEO owns AI risk, and staff review high-impact output.[^20][^1]

headings.what-it-is: What is a fractional chief AI officer, and what does it change?
headings.faq: Questions buyers ask about a fractional chief AI officer

answers.walk-away: You should walk away with a written mandate, an inventory of AI in use, one redesigned workflow, a skills plan and a dated decision on the seat.[^1][^17]
answers.spokes: Most firms need four kinds of help around this seat: a plan, AI rules, staff adoption and the build of the first workflow.[^1][^18]
answers.human-role: Your CEO keeps AI risk decisions, and process owners, the IT lead and the staff who use the tools keep theirs.[^20][^1]
answers.recipes: The work takes three shapes: a dedicated part-time owner, an existing executive with outside support, or a full-time hire.[^1][^2]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI leadership stalls when the owner lacks authority or time, the problem is unclear, or trials never end.[^8][^18]
answers.benchmark: Judge a fractional AI chief on a written mandate, a sample AI inventory, named risk owners and a day-90 decision, not on a slide deck.[^1][^20]
answers.something-else: Skip paid AI leadership when free public advisers, an existing executive with protected time, or a one-off plan will do.[^22][^2]

summary: A fractional chief AI officer is a part-time executive who owns a firm's AI decisions, risks and staff adoption.[^1][^16] What changes is ownership: one person keeps the AI inventory, runs risk reviews and decides what ships.[^1][^20] Real authority and protected time make or break it.[^8][^4]
walkAway: A written mandate: decision rights, a budget line and authority to stop projects.[^5] In IBM's vendor survey, only 18% of chief AI officers fully control AI investment.[^8]
An inventory of the AI already in use, each given a risk tier: how much harm a mistake could do.[^1][^20] The federal job description makes the inventory a core duty.[^1]
One or two workflows redesigned with the team that does them, then measured against a baseline.[^18] Measures matter: the average firm scrapped 46% of its AI trial projects.[^19]
A skills plan, so AI adds to what staff can do.[^1] Free training comes through AI U, run by America's Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), and the US Chamber.[^22][^24]
A decision, by an agreed date, on whether the seat goes full-time, stays part-time or ends.[^17] Research on interim leaders puts succession among the core factors.[^17]

spokes.why: Sets which workflow goes first and its measure. Misreading the problem is RAND's top cause of AI project failure.[^18]
Sets which rules apply and who signs off: the owner's risk duty.[^1][^20]
Gets staff using AI in real work, so trials don't stall: firms scrapped 46% of AI trial projects on average.[^19]
Builds staff skills, a core duty in the federal job description.[^1]
Redesigns and builds the first workflow once the owner picks it.[^1][^18]
For the COO who may hold the AI seat alongside the day job.[^2][^4]

humanRole: CEO or owner: keeps accountability for AI risk decisions.[^20] Even in federal agencies, the AI chief advises the agency head, who stays in charge.[^1]
Process owner (COO, ops lead, controller): owns each redesigned workflow and its result.[^1] Federal rules give risk duties to whoever answers for the outcome.[^1]
IT lead: owns data access, security and vendor setup.[^20] Write down where that job ends and the AI chief's begins.[^20][^21]
Staff who use the tools: review high-impact output before it counts.[^1] In IBM's vendor survey, 73% of AI chiefs define where human oversight is non-negotiable.[^8]

recipes.name: 1. Dedicated part-time owner, for a fixed term
recipes.when: AI is in use across teams, but no executive owns it.[^13] Census found 32% of US firms with 100 to 249 staff use AI, and 37% with 250+.[^13]
flow: CEO: write the mandate, decision rights and stop authority
Fractional AI officer: build the AI inventory and risk tiers in month one
Process owner: pick one workflow in one team or site, and agree a growth measure such as orders handled, not just hours saved
IT lead: approve one AI platform and set who can access what
Staff: review high-impact output as the new workflow runs
CEO: review at day 90 and decide full-time, extend or end
recipes.cost: Weigh it against a full-time seat: about $251,000 to $259,000 a year at median US IT-manager pay plus benefits.[^9][^10][^11] Ask for a fixed term and a fixed scope.

recipes.name: 2. Existing executive takes the seat, with outside support
recipes.when: A COO or IT lead already has the CEO's trust and can free up real time.[^16][^4] Most federal chief AI officers hold the job alongside another, as at DHS and USDA.[^2][^3][^7]
flow: CEO: name the executive and protect a fixed share of their week
Named executive: own priorities, decisions and the risk review
Outside adviser: build the AI inventory and draft the AI policy
Process owner: run the first workflow and report its measure
Staff: take free training through an SBDC or, for manufacturers, a Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) center
recipes.cost: No new salary; the hidden cost is the executive's time, and limited time hinders execution.[^4] Free help comes from SBDC AI U and MEP centers.[^22][^23]

recipes.name: 3. Full-time hire, when AI is core to what you sell
recipes.when: AI is part of your product, or several high-impact uses need daily ownership.[^1][^20]
flow: CEO: write the mandate and reporting line before the search starts
Owner or board: set the budget and decision rights
New AI chief: take over the inventory and risk reviews
Process owners: keep owning their workflows and results
recipes.cost: About $251,000 to $259,000 a year at median US IT-manager pay plus benefits.[^9][^10][^11] Public-company AI chiefs cost far more: Equilar, a pay-data firm, puts their median total pay at $1.9 million.[^12]

ownData.title: Which part-time executive seats do US firms advertise?
ownData.intro: US firms advertise part-time finance seats far more than part-time AI leaders: we found 98 fractional CFO ads but only 3 for an AI leader.[^27][^28] None of the 3 was a firm of 40 to 500 staff hiring for its own seat.[^27] We counted US job ads with "fractional" in the title, by seat, in two job-ad indexes, over the 90 days to 26 Nov 2026.[^28][^29]
rows: AI, data or machine learning lead
ownData.note: Source: Zavient count in the JobsPipe and Hirebase indexes, pulled 26 Nov 2026; Lightcast, a labor-data vendor, also finds finance is 46% of fractional postings.[^27][^28][^29][^14] Counts are approximate, titles overlap, the "any" row includes uses like fractional aircraft, and agency reposts are included. An ad is not a hire, and forum posters say such seats fill through connections.[^25]

watchOuts: Title without authority: in IBM's vendor survey, only 18% of AI chiefs fully control AI investment.[^8] Fix: put the budget and stop authority in writing.[^5]
Add-on owner, no time: among firms over 1,000 staff, 58% with a newly named AI chief report strong returns, against 24% with an add-on.[^6] Fix: protect a fixed share of the owner's week.[^4]
Unclear problem or measure: RAND's top root cause of AI project failure is leaders misreading the problem.[^18] Fix: write the business problem and its measure before choosing a tool.
Trials that never ship: S&P Global found 42% of firms abandoned most AI initiatives, up from 17%.[^19] Fix: give every trial a go-or-stop date.
Low trust: trust and top-team backing are the top success factors for part-time tech chiefs.[^16] Fix: check references on trust, and have the CEO back the owner openly.
No exit plan: research on interim leaders lists succession as a core factor.[^17] Fix: agree the handover plan in month one.
howToTest: Write the mandate first: decision rights, stop authority and a budget line.[^8][^5]
Ask for a sample AI inventory and the method they use to tier risk.[^1][^20]
Ask who they would name for each risk decision.[^20][^21]
Ask which workflow they would redesign first, and the growth measure they would track.[^18]
Ask what they would stop in the first 90 days, and why. In IBM's vendor survey, high-impact AI chiefs stop failing projects 96% of the time, against 46%.[^8]
Check fit with your IT lead: agree in writing who owns data, security and vendors.[^20]
Agree how often they meet the CEO. Federal rules require regular contact with agency leaders.[^1]
Set a day-90 review with three outcomes: full-time, extend or end.[^17]
Call references from clients of your size, and ask about trust and integrity.[^16]
If an insider takes the seat instead, hold their plan to the same checks.[^1][^4]

faq.q: What does a fractional chief AI officer do?
faq.a: A fractional chief AI officer owns a firm's AI decisions part-time: the AI inventory, risk reviews, staff skills and advice to the CEO.[^1] The federal job description lists the same duties.[^1][^2]

faq.q: How is a fractional chief AI officer different from an AI consultant?
faq.a: A consultant delivers a project; a fractional AI chief owns decisions over time.[^15][^16] Research on part-time IT chiefs finds roles from adviser to full owner, so agree which one you're buying.[^16]

faq.q: Does a company of 40 to 500 people need a chief AI officer?
faq.a: Only if AI is in use across teams with no clear owner; you need an owner, not a title.[^1][^20] Census found 32% of US firms with 100 to 249 staff use AI.[^13] Federal rules let an existing executive hold the role.[^1]

faq.q: Fractional or full-time chief AI officer: which fits?
faq.a: Part-time or add-on fits while AI uses are few and you need an owner more than a team.[^1][^2] Go full-time once AI is core to what you sell, or several high-impact uses need daily care.[^1][^20]

faq.q: How much does a chief AI officer cost?
faq.a: A full-time seat costs about $251,000 to $259,000 a year at median US IT-manager pay plus benefits.[^9][^10][^11] Method: median pay of $175,140 divided by the wage share of total pay, 67.5% to 69.7%.[^9][^10][^11] Public-company AI chiefs get far more: a median $1.9 million in total pay, per Equilar, a pay-data firm.[^12]

faq.q: How do we judge a fractional chief AI officer in the first 90 days?
faq.a: Judge them at day 90 on a written mandate, an AI inventory with risk tiers, one measured workflow and a decision on the seat.[^1][^17] A deck with no named owners is a red flag.[^20]

pickElse: Just starting, with little AI in use: use free public help first, such as SBDC AI U or an MEP center.[^22][^23] One forum reply says part-time AI leadership fits once AI shows business value.[^26]

An executive already has trust and spare time: give them the seat and protect part of their week.[^2][^4] Use the free AI Risk Management Framework Playbook from NIST, the US standards body, as their checklist.[^20]
You need a plan, not an owner: buy a one-off strategy engagement with a clear problem and measure.[^18] Then hand the plan to an internal owner.
AI is core to what you sell, with many high-impact uses: hire full-time instead.[^1][^9]

offer.heading: Not sure who should own AI here? Get a free 30-minute diagnostic
offer.body: Free, before any paid work: 30 minutes on who owns AI at your firm today. Bring a list of the AI tools your teams use. You leave knowing whether a part-time owner, an existing executive or a full-time hire fits.

reviews.notes: Read as the likely add-on owner. The job-ad table landed because its intro says the so-what first. 'Growth measure' was vague; recipe 1 now gives an example (orders handled) and says not just hours saved. No source gives a share of the week to protect, so the page says 'a fixed share' rather than inventing one.

Tripped on SBDC, MEP, NIST AI RMF and 'risk tier'. Each is now spelled out or glossed on first use: risk tier means how much harm a mistake could do. Step flows name a role on every line and read fine on a phone.

Wanted to know whether one unit can go first; recipe 1 now picks one workflow in one team or site. The full-time cost is labelled as IT-manager pay plus benefits with the method shown, which is the comparison a GM would make. No fractional fee is given, by design.

Read as the COO or IT lead who might hold the seat in recipe 2. The checks only judged an outsider; added a tenth: hold an insider's plan to the same checks. The add-on watch-out, with its over-1,000-staff caveat, is the honest warning this reader needs.

Steve asks first whether he needs one at all; FAQ 3 answers 'only if' and says he needs an owner, not a title. Equilar meant nothing to him, so it is now glossed as a pay-data firm. The strategy-engagement alternative now reads as two short sentences. The offer asks for a list of AI tools in use, which he can bring cold.
